templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Colon between independent clauses (second explains first)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long noun-phrase opener
items.passage: In 2010, astronomers using NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope identified two enormous ______ of high-energy radiation extending roughly 25,000 light-years above and below the galactic plane, the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated in an outburst from the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way’s center.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “astronomers using NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope identified two enormous structures.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “Lobes of high-energy radiation extending roughly 25,000 light-years above and below the galactic plane,” which describes its subject, “the so-called Fermi bubbles,” and then gives the main verb “may have originated.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “lobes of high-energy radiation ...” an appositive describing the structures in the first sentence, so the main clause “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated ...” is joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “structures lobes of high-energy radiation” runs two nouns together inside the first sentence, and the main clause “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated ...” then follows it with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which are lobes ...” turns the phrase into a relative clause describing the structures, so the main clause “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Fermi bubbles, two gamma-ray lobes reported in 2010 from Fermi telescope data, each extending about 25,000 light-years from the galactic plane; origin possibly an outburst from Sagittarius A*, stated with may). Known facts, no names. Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): article-less noun-phrase opener of 14 words that reads naturally as an appositive to clause 1's last noun (two enormous structures, lobes of ...), the 940ff6f7 shape; the comma, glued and which options all hold until the splice at “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated,” 14 to 18 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 46 words; reasoning steps 3.
band7_moves: opener of 14 words, an article-less noun-phrase appositive that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (two enormous structures, lobes of high-energy radiation ...)
comma, glued and which options hold until the splice at “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated,” 14 to 18 words after the blank

band7.why: 14-word article-less noun-phrase opener (Lobes of high-energy radiation ...) reads naturally as an appositive to clause 1's last noun, the 940ff6f7 shape; comma, glued and which options all hold until “the so-called Fermi bubbles may have originated,” 14 to 18 words past the blank; 46-word run

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a participial opener
items.passage: Accidentally imported from Asia, the fungus that causes chestnut blight was first discovered in 1904 infecting American chestnut trees at New York’s Bronx ______ rapidly southward along the Appalachian Mountains, the disease had killed an estimated three billion chestnuts by 1950.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “was first discovered in 1904 infecting American chestnut trees at New York’s Bronx Zoo.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Spreading rapidly southward along the Appalachian Mountains,” which describes its subject, “the disease,” and then gives the verb “had killed.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “spreading rapidly southward ...” describe the fungus at the end of the first sentence, so the main clause “the disease had killed an estimated three billion chestnuts by 1950” is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “trees at New York’s Bronx Zoo spreading rapidly southward ...” attaches the participial phrase to the first sentence, and the main clause “the disease had killed ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” joins “spreading rapidly southward ...” to “infecting American chestnut trees” as a second description of the fungus, so the main clause “the disease had killed ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (chestnut blight, Cryphonectria parasitica, from Asia, first noticed in 1904 at the New York Zoological Park in the Bronx; it spread through the Appalachians and killed some three to four billion American chestnuts by about 1950). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape (886dc9f9 menu, `Bay and having`): 6-word participial opener that reads naturally as a trailing modifier of the fungus (discovered ... infecting trees ..., spreading rapidly southward); splice at “the disease had killed,” 7 words after the blank. One-sentence run of 41 words. Participial opener, so it differs from the noun-phrase opener of w5b5_01.

band7.why: 6-word participial opener that reads as a trailing modifier of the fungus, splice 7 words past the blank; 886dc9f9 band-6 menu, band_target 6

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause (instead)
items.passage: Many bioluminescent ostracods, tiny crustaceans related to shrimp, emit light only defensively, releasing luminous mucus to startle predators. Males of several Caribbean species don’t reserve their light for ______ they release glowing dots in species-specific sequences while swimming after dark, displays that females use to locate potential mates.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both “Males of several Caribbean species don’t reserve their light for emergencies” and “they release glowing dots in species-specific sequences ...” are main clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them, and the comma after “instead” sets off the adverb that opens the second clause, which tells what the males do in place of reserving their light.

B.why_wrong: The commas set off “instead,” but nothing joins the two main clauses except a comma, a comma splice; a conjunctive adverb like “instead” cannot join clauses the way “and” or “but” can.

C.why_wrong: Placing “instead” at the end of the first clause leaves only a comma between the main clauses “Males of several Caribbean species don’t reserve their light for emergencies instead” and “they release glowing dots ...,” a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone joins the two main clauses “Males of several Caribbean species don’t reserve their light for emergencies” and “they release glowing dots ...,” a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Caribbean ostracods, or sea fireflies: many cypridinid ostracods release luminous mucus as a defense; in Caribbean species males court with trains of glowing mucus dots whose spacing and timing differ by species, and females use them to find males). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape (a9e5b788 `; rather,` menu): key `L; instead, R`; the adverb opens clause 2 because that clause says what the males do in place of what clause 1 denies. Three splices in different disguises (band 6 stacks splices). Run 30 words. No logic-wrong option (that is the band-7 shape, used in w5b5_04).

band7.why: `; instead,` key with three splices in different disguises and no logic-wrong option, the a9e5b788 band-6 shape; band_target 6

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause (though) and answering the previous sentence
items.passage: Adult mayflies are notoriously short-lived, most surviving only a day or two after emerging from the water. Considered in its entirety, a mayfly’s life is far from ______ the insect typically spends a year or more developing underwater as a nymph, grazing on algae and molting repeatedly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adverb “though” belongs to the clause “Considered in its entirety, a mayfly’s life is far from brief, though,” which is contrary to what the previous sentence suggests (that mayflies live only a day or two). A comma separates “though” from that clause, and a semicolon joins it to the next main clause, “the insect typically spends a year or more developing underwater as a nymph ...,” which explains why the whole life is not brief.

A.why_wrong: Placing the semicolon before “though” makes “though the insect typically spends a year or more developing underwater as a nymph ...” a subordinate clause standing alone after a semicolon, and it illogically presents the long nymph stage as contrary to the claim that a mayfly’s life is far from brief, when it is the reason for that claim.

B.why_wrong: The commas set off “though,” but the main clauses “a mayfly’s life is far from brief” and “the insect typically spends a year or more ...” are then joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark after it, “though” becomes a subordinating conjunction, which illogically presents the year spent developing as a nymph as contrary to the claim that a mayfly’s life is far from brief, when it is the reason for that claim.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (mayflies, order Ephemeroptera: adults live from minutes to a day or two; nymphs live in water for months to two years, typically about a year, grazing on algae and molting many times). Known facts, no names. Band-7 checks: key `L, though; R` with the adverb closing clause 1, and clause 1 contradicts the expectation set by the previous sentence (short-lived adults vs a long life taken whole); two logic-wrong options (`; though` and `, though` as a subordinator, as CB's own rationale for 5aa171de rejects them) plus the splice `, though,`; the cue is in the previous sentence, outside a 6-word window; run 30 words. Frame differs from 5aa171de (no “hardly”).
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 (`L, though; R`) and clause 1 contradicts the expectation set by the previous sentence
two logic-wrong distractors (`L; though R`, `L, though R`) that fail only against the previous sentence
cue in the previous sentence, outside a 6-word window

band7.why: key `L, though; R` closes clause 1, which corrects the previous sentence; two logic-wrong options (`; though` and `, though` as a subordinator) rejected as CB's own rationale for 5aa171de rejects them, plus the `, though,` splice; the cue sits in the previous sentence, outside a 6-word window

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive appositive (title + name) before the verb
items.passage: To make A Colour Box (1935), an advertisement for the parcel service of Britain’s General Post Office, New Zealand–born ______ painted vibrant abstract patterns directly onto celluloid instead of using a camera, synchronizing their rhythms with a popular dance tune.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “New Zealand–born filmmaker” is a title that comes right before the name “Len Lye” with no article, so the name is essential and no comma belongs between them. No comma belongs between the subject “New Zealand–born filmmaker Len Lye” and its verb, “painted,” either.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “New Zealand–born filmmaker” from the name it identifies, “Len Lye.” An article-less title before a name forms a single unit with the name.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject “New Zealand–born filmmaker Len Lye” from its verb, “painted.”

D.why_wrong: The pair of commas treats “Len Lye” as extra information that could be removed, but without the name the sentence would read “New Zealand–born filmmaker painted,” which lacks the essential identification.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Len Lye, A Colour Box, 1935, made for the GPO Film Unit by painting directly on film; it advertises the cheaper parcel post and is cut to a Cuban dance number). Known facts. Band-7 checks: title + name followed straight by the verb, after a long introductory phrase that ends in a comma, so the `Len Lye,` option looks like the close of a polite appositive; the compound title (New Zealand–born filmmaker) reads like a description a comma might follow; S4_restrictive is local at every band (section 6 exempts it from the window check). One-sentence run of 40 words.
band7_moves: title + name followed by the verb, which tempts a comma after the name (`filmmaker Len Lye,`)
commas around the name (`filmmaker, Len Lye,`), the hardest distractor for the template at band 7
long introductory phrase with its own appositive before the title, so commas are already flowing when the blank arrives

band7.why: nationality plus occupation title with the name as subject and the verb right after it, behind a 20-word introductory phrase that ends in a comma; full four-way comma menu as in 5aae2475 and 960dec02 (S4_restrictive is local at every band)

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive appositive (title + name) after a preposition
items.passage: Humpback whales have rounded bumps called tubercles along the leading edges of their flippers. Wind tunnel experiments by ______ and his colleagues demonstrated that a model flipper fitted with tubercles can reach steeper angles before stalling, a finding later applied to wind turbine engineering.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Biologist” is a title that comes right before the name “Frank Fish” with no article, so the name is essential and no comma belongs between them. “Biologist Frank Fish and his colleagues” is the object of “by,” and no comma belongs before the “and” that joins its two parts.

A.why_wrong: The commas treat “Frank Fish” as removable extra information, but “experiments by biologist and his colleagues” does not identify who ran the experiments; the name is essential to the title before it.

C.why_wrong: The comma separates “biologist Frank Fish” from “and his colleagues,” the other half of the compound object of “by”; no comma belongs inside a two-part compound joined by “and.”

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between the preposition “by” and the name that completes its object; what comes before the colon is not a complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and technology (humpback flipper tubercles; wind tunnel tests published in 2004 by Miklosovic, Murray, Howle and biologist Frank Fish of West Chester University found the bumpy model stalled at a steeper angle; applied to WhalePower turbine blades). Known facts; “and his colleagues” keeps the credit shared. Band-6 shape (80aa7690, 4dcedc31): title + name as the object of a preposition, followed by `and his colleagues`, which tempts a comma after the name. Review split the tubercle definition into its own sentence; run now 30 words (S4_restrictive is local at every band).

fixes: split the 44-word sentence: the tubercle definition is now its own opening sentence (register: words per sentence above CB)

band7.why: title + name as the object of “by,” followed by “and his colleagues,” which tempts a comma; 80aa7690 band-6 shape, band_target 6

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a specified item
items.passage: Since the eighth century, the Shōsōin, a wooden storehouse at the Tōdai-ji temple in Nara, Japan, has preserved musical instruments, textiles, and glassware. Some of these objects were imported from as far away as Persia. The core of this collection was given in 756 by a single ______ Empress Kōmyō, who dedicated her late husband’s possessions to the temple.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The core of this collection was given in 756 by a single benefactor” is complete, and what follows names that benefactor: “Empress Kōmyō, who dedicated her late husband’s possessions to the temple.” A colon correctly introduces this specification.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “Empress Kōmyō, who dedicated her late husband’s possessions to the temple” is a noun phrase with a relative clause, not a main clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Empress Kōmyō, who dedicated her late husband’s possessions to the temple” as a fragment: its only verb, “dedicated,” belongs to the relative clause.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “a single benefactor Empress Kōmyō” runs the noun into the name that specifies it; a mark is needed to introduce the specification.

items.notes: Subject: history (Shōsōin, the treasure house of Tōdai-ji in Nara; in 756, after Emperor Shōmu's death, Empress Kōmyō dedicated his belongings to the temple's Great Buddha, and these form the core of the collection, which includes Sasanian glass and musical instruments). Known facts. The name appears in a live Rhetorical Synthesis item only inside a source note, not as its subject. Band-6 shape (c468db1c): an announcing noun (a single benefactor) then the specified item with a relative clause holding a finite verb, so the period and semicolon options look possible. No plain comma option (a comma appositive would be acceptable there). Run 24 words.

fixes: split the 32-word opening sentence: the Persian imports are now their own sentence (register)

band7.why: announcing noun (a single benefactor) then the named item with a relative clause holding a finite verb; c468db1c single-mark band-6 menu, band_target 6

items.subtype: Closing dash of a pair, with a parenthetical nested inside the dash element
items.passage: Covered with roughly 2,200 glyphs chronicling the dynastic history of Copán, a powerful Maya kingdom that flourished in present-day western Honduras, its Hieroglyphic Stairway—dedicated in 755 CE by the ruler K’ak’ Yipyaj Chan K’awiil (Smoke ______ is the longest known inscription produced by the ancient Maya.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “its Hieroglyphic Stairway” opens a supplementary element, “dedicated in 755 CE by the ruler K’ak’ Yipyaj Chan K’awiil (Smoke Shell),” that must be closed by a second dash before the main verb, “is.” The closing parenthesis ends the nickname inside that element, and the dash then closes the element itself.

B.why_wrong: The parenthesis closes the nickname, but nothing closes the element opened by the dash after “its Hieroglyphic Stairway,” so the supplement runs straight into the verb “is.”

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot close an element that was opened with a dash; the supplement “dedicated in 755 CE by the ruler ...” must end with a matching dash.

D.why_wrong: The comma inside the parenthesis has no role there, and nothing closes the element opened by the dash after “its Hieroglyphic Stairway.”

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Hieroglyphic Stairway at Copán, western Honduras, about 2,200 glyphs on 62 steps, the longest known Maya inscription, recording the city's dynastic history; dedicated in 755 CE by the fifteenth ruler, K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil, called Smoke Shell). Known facts. Band-7 checks: two levels of supplement (a parenthetical nickname nested inside a dash element, the 83898524 menu); the opening dash is 12 words before the blank, outside a 6-word window; the element sits between subject and verb, so the options that do not close it still read on to “is”; reasoning steps 4 (left side, right side, partner elsewhere, two slots varying). One-sentence run of 46 words.
band7_moves: two levels of supplement: a parenthetical nickname nested inside a dash element
opening dash 12 words before the blank, outside a 6-word window
options mix the levels (parenthesis alone, parenthesis plus comma, comma inside the parenthesis)

band7.why: parenthetical nickname nested inside a dash element that sits between subject and verb, opening dash 12 words before the blank; the four options are the same shapes as 83898524 (by design), so the student must track both levels

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: The Mercury 13, women aviators who passed the same physiological screening as NASA’s Mercury astronauts, included Jerrie Cobb, the first candidate to complete the ______ a mother of eight married to a US senator; and Wally Funk, who finally traveled to space in 2021 at age eighty-two.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three women, and each item carries its own comma-set description (“Jerrie Cobb, the first candidate to complete the screening”), so semicolons must separate the items, as the semicolon before “and Wally Funk” shows. A semicolon after “screening” ends the first item, and a comma after “Janey Hart” sets off her description, “a mother of eight married to a US senator.”

A.why_wrong: Commas after “screening” and “Janey Hart” blur the first two items into one string of names and descriptions, and they do not match the semicolon that separates the last item.

B.why_wrong: The semicolon after “screening” is right, but with no comma after “Janey Hart,” her name runs into the description “a mother of eight married to a US senator.”

D.why_wrong: The semicolon falls in the wrong slot: it cuts “Janey Hart” off from her own description, “a mother of eight married to a US senator,” while a comma is left between the first and second items.

items.notes: Subject: history (Mercury 13: women pilots who in 1960 and 1961 passed the Lovelace Clinic screening used for the Mercury astronauts; Jerrie Cobb first; Janey Hart, mother of eight and wife of Senator Philip Hart; Wally Funk flew on Blue Origin in July 2021 at 82). Known facts. Band-6 shape (a8fa749a menu): blank spans the series mark and the comma after the next item's head, both slots vary; the revealing semicolon comes later (before “and Wally Funk”). One-sentence run of 47 words.

band7.why: semicolon series with both slots varying and the revealing semicolon later in the sentence; a8fa749a band-6 menu, band_target 6

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction before a clause that opens with a subordinate clause
items.passage: In 1991, two South African engineers developed the Hippo Roller, a 90-liter drum that transports water by rolling along the ground, pushed with a steel ______ because the ground rather than the carrier supports the weight, each trip can deliver several times more water than a traditional bucket.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1991, two South African engineers developed the Hippo Roller ...” and “because the ground rather than the carrier supports the weight, each trip can deliver several times more water than a traditional bucket” are both main clauses (the second opens with a subordinate “because” clause). A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two long main clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: The comma alone joins the two main clauses; read with the comma, “because the ground rather than the carrier supports the weight” attaches to the first sentence, and “each trip can deliver ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: social science and technology (Hippo Roller, a 90-liter rolling water drum with a push handle, designed in South Africa in 1991; lets one person move several times the water of a bucket). Known facts; the designers are left unnamed. Band-6 shape (59094d87, 7ce4ee13 menu): clause 2 opens with a 10-word because-clause, so the comma option reads as a trailing because-clause until “each trip can deliver.” One-sentence run of 48 words. No band-7 version exists for the template.

fixes: “propelled by a steel handle” changed to “pushed with a steel handle” (a person pushes, the handle does not propel)

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 (a 10-word because-clause opens clause 2 and reads as trailing until “each trip can deliver”)

items.subtype: Colon between independent clauses when the second opens with whereas
items.passage: An experimental finding that psychologists call the Baker-baker paradox reveals a curious inconsistency in human ______ whereas participants shown a stranger’s photograph and told that he is a baker usually remember that information later, those told that his surname is Baker frequently forget it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first clause, “An experimental finding that psychologists call the Baker-baker paradox reveals a curious inconsistency in human memory,” is complete, and the second, “whereas participants shown a stranger’s photograph and told that he is a baker usually remember that information later, those told that his surname is Baker frequently forget it,” is also a main clause (its subject and verb are “those ... forget”) that explains what the inconsistency is. A colon correctly joins the clauses and introduces this explanation.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the main clause ending “human memory” and the main clause “those told that his surname is Baker frequently forget it” (with its “whereas” clause) are fused into a run-on sentence.

B.why_wrong: The comma joins two main clauses, “An experimental finding that psychologists call the Baker-baker paradox reveals a curious inconsistency in human memory” and “whereas participants shown a stranger’s photograph ... those told that his surname is Baker frequently forget it,” with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, “and” cannot join two long main clauses like these, and “and” presents the second clause as a further point rather than as the explanation of the inconsistency that the first clause announces.

items.notes: Subject: social science (the Baker-baker paradox in memory research, McWeeny, Young, Hay and Ellis 1987: people shown a face later recall that the person is a baker more often than that his surname is Baker). Known facts, no names. Review replaced the Wason selection task (textbook-famous; claimed in claims.txt, Wason withdrawn). Band-7 checks: clause 1 announces (a curious inconsistency); clause 2 opens with “whereas,” so it looks dependent and the comma option looks legal (bb4557cf, 9579581e); the `and` decoy is wrong by relation as well as by the missing comma; the splice in the comma option shows only at “those told,” 18 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 44 words.
band7_moves: clause 2 opens with a whereas-clause, so it looks dependent and the comma option looks legal
relation-wrong decoy (`L and R`) beside the colon key
splice shows only at “most succeed,” 13 words after the blank; run of 50 words

fixes: replaced the subject: the Wason selection task is textbook-famous (fame call asked for); new subject the Baker-baker paradox (grepped bank, officials, rounds; claimed, Wason withdrawn), same bb4557cf shape, option menu and key D; run 44 words instead of 50

band7.why: rebuilt on the Baker-baker paradox: clause 1 announces (a curious inconsistency), clause 2 opens with “whereas” so the comma looks legal, the `and` decoy fails on relation as well as punctuation; splice shows 18 words past the blank; 44-word run; bb4557cf and 9579581e shape

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In the late 1800s, residents of Boonville, a farming town in California’s Anderson Valley, invented a jargon called Boontling, reportedly so they could talk privately in front of outsiders. Its vocabulary eventually exceeded a thousand ______ only a handful of residents remain fluent today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its vocabulary eventually exceeded a thousand words” and “only a handful of residents remain fluent today” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast.

B.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone joins the main clauses “Its vocabulary eventually exceeded a thousand words” and “only a handful of residents remain fluent today,” a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: language (Boontling, the jargon of Boonville, Anderson Valley, Mendocino County, California, developed from the 1880s, some 1,000 to 1,200 words; few fluent speakers today). Known facts, no names. Medium shape (870ae7ec menu): short clauses, the second opening with its subject.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around an appositive
items.passage: Chungking Mansions, a seventeen-story building in Hong Kong crowded with cheap guesthouses, phone shops, and curry ______ is described by anthropologist Gordon Mathews as a center of “low-end globalization.” Traders from South Asia and Africa stay there while buying goods to resell back home.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “Chungking Mansions” opens the appositive “a seventeen-story building in Hong Kong crowded with cheap guesthouses, phone shops, and curry restaurants.” A second comma is needed to close it before the verb “is described.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the appositive opened by the comma after “Chungking Mansions” never ends, and the series “guesthouses, phone shops, and curry restaurants” runs straight into the verb “is described.”

C.why_wrong: A dash cannot close an element that was opened with a comma; the appositive must end with a matching comma.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot separate the subject “Chungking Mansions” and its appositive from the verb “is described”; neither side is a main clause.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Chungking Mansions, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong; anthropologist Gordon Mathews, Ghetto at the Center of the World, 2011, calls it a hub of low-end globalization where South Asian and African traders buy goods such as phones to resell). Known facts. Medium shape (7f48b098): the opening comma is 14 words before the blank, and series commas inside the appositive tempt the missing-comma option.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses, second opening with a short introductory phrase
items.passage: In 2001, Hungarian architect Áron Losonczi developed LiTraCon, a translucent building material made by embedding thousands of optical glass fibers in ______ to these fibers, which transmit light from one surface of a block to the opposite surface, a LiTraCon wall reveals the silhouettes of people standing behind it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a translucent building material made by embedding thousands of optical glass fibers in concrete.” The second sentence opens with the introductory phrase “Thanks to these fibers,” followed by a “which” clause about the fibers, its subject, “a LiTraCon wall,” and its verb, “reveals.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “a LiTraCon wall reveals the silhouettes ...” to the main clause “Hungarian architect Áron Losonczi developed LiTraCon ...” with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “embedding thousands of optical glass fibers in concrete thanks to these fibers” attaches the phrase to the first sentence, and the main clause “a LiTraCon wall reveals ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which thanks to these fibers” begins a relative clause about the concrete that never gets its own verb before the new subject “a LiTraCon wall,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: technology (LiTraCon, light-transmitting concrete with embedded optical glass fibers, developed in 2001 by Hungarian architect Áron Losonczi; shadows on one side show through). Known facts. Medium shape (01a32c84, 2c84f96a): 3-word introductory phrase after the period key, plus a which-clause before clause 2's subject.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing sentence appositive
items.passage: Statues made of Coade stone, an artificial material produced at Eleanor Coade’s London factory in the late 1700s, still look remarkably fresh after two centuries outdoors. Workers pressed a mixture of clay, flint, and glass into molds and fired the pieces in a ______ a process that left them harder and less porous than most natural stone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with “Workers pressed a mixture of clay, flint, and glass into molds and fired the pieces in a kiln.” What follows, “a process that left them harder and less porous than most natural stone,” is a noun phrase that sums up that procedure. A comma correctly sets off this trailing element from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a process that left them harder and less porous than most natural stone” is a noun phrase, not a main clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “A process that left them harder and less porous than most natural stone” as a fragment: its only verb, “left,” belongs to the “that” clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, “in a kiln a process ...” runs the trailing noun phrase into the main clause with nothing to set it off.

items.notes: Subject: arts and technology (Coade stone, the fired ceramic made at Eleanor Coade's factory in Lambeth, London, from 1769: clay, grog, flint and crushed glass pressed into molds and fired for days, so durable that many statues and ornaments still stand outdoors). Known facts, no study claims. Review replaced the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (script and alphabet origins already fill about a dozen live items: N’Ko, Glagolitic, Tifinagh, Ogham, Osmanya, Adlam, Ugaritic, Mongolian; claimed, the old subject withdrawn). Medium shape (3ed5ebb4, 8f6d6ae6, a sentence appositive): the appositive carries its own that-clause with a finite verb, so period and semicolon options look possible. 57 words against the models' median of 56.

fixes: replaced the subject: script and alphabet origins already fill about a dozen live items; new subject Coade stone (grepped bank, officials, rounds; claimed, old subject withdrawn), same sentence-appositive shape and key D, 57 words

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: The parasitic crustacean that enters a spotted rose snapper through its gills and then clamps onto the base of the fish’s ______ gradually cuts off the organ’s blood supply; once the tongue withers away, the parasite attaches itself to the stub and functions as a replacement tongue.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first clause is the long noun phrase “The parasitic crustacean that enters a spotted rose snapper through its gills and then clamps onto the base of the fish’s tongue,” and its verb is “cuts off.” No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, which ends with “the base of the fish’s tongue,” from its verb, “gradually cuts off.”

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “The parasitic crustacean that enters ... the fish’s tongue” is only a subject with no main verb yet.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before it are only a subject; the verb “cuts off” is on the other side.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Cymothoa exigua, the tongue-eating louse, a parasitic isopod of the eastern Pacific: it enters through the gills, the female attaches to the tongue of a spotted rose snapper, the tongue atrophies, and the isopod attaches to the stub and serves as the tongue). Known facts, no names. Medium shape (be34a3df, 403d7bb5): a 22-word subject with a relative clause, ending in a noun, so a comma feels natural before the verb.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: Akrotiri, a Bronze Age town on the Greek island of Santorini, was buried by volcanic ash around 1600 BCE. Excavators there have uncovered multistory houses with brightly painted walls but almost no human ______ it appears that the town’s residents had fled before the eruption, perhaps warned by preceding earthquakes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Excavators there have uncovered multistory houses with brightly painted walls but almost no human remains” and “it appears that the town’s residents had fled before the eruption” are both main clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone joins the main clauses ending “almost no human remains” and “it appears that the town’s residents had fled ...,” a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period ends the first sentence correctly, but adding “Because” turns the second sentence into a fragment: “Because it appears that the town’s residents had fled before the eruption, perhaps warned by preceding earthquakes” is a dependent clause with no main clause.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Akrotiri, Santorini, buried by the Minoan eruption around 1600 BCE; multistory houses and frescoes; almost no human remains or valuables, so residents probably left after warning earthquakes). Known facts, hedged (it appears, perhaps). Medium shape (4ba99a6f menu, with an added-word option, `. Because`, in place of `later`; clause 2 opens with “it appears that” so the no-mark option cannot be read as a reduced relative clause): review moved the burial into its own opening sentence (register), so the blank sentence is a 31-word run.

fixes: split the 51-word sentence: Akrotiri's burial is now its own opening sentence (register); explanation quote updated

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In his 1933 essay In Praise of Shadows, Japanese novelist Jun’ichirō Tanizaki argues that traditional Japanese architecture and crafts were designed to be appreciated in dim light. Lacquerware, he writes, reveals its true beauty only in the flickering glow ______ a candle.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A candle” is the object of the preposition “of,” and no punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between the preposition “of” and its object, “a candle”; what comes before the colon is not a complete clause.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “of” from its object, “a candle.”

D.why_wrong: A dash has no role between the preposition “of” and its object, “a candle.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Jun'ichirō Tanizaki, In'ei Raisan, In Praise of Shadows, 1933 essay; lacquerware is meant to be seen by candlelight or lamplight in dim rooms). Known facts. Easy shape (a1e0c981 menu).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: During Japan’s Kofun period (about 250–600 CE), powerful leaders were buried in enormous earthen mounds known as kofun. Hollow terracotta figures called haniwa were arranged in rows on these mounds, and the figures ______ warriors, horses, houses, and even musicians.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Warriors, horses, houses, and even musicians” is the object of the verb “depicted,” and no punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “the figures depicted” is not complete without its object; a colon cannot separate a verb from its object.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the verb “depicted” from its object, “warriors, horses, houses, and even musicians.”

C.why_wrong: A dash has no role between the verb “depicted” and its object.

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (haniwa, hollow terracotta figures set on Kofun-period burial mounds, about 250 to 600 CE: cylinders, houses, horses, warriors, musicians, dancers). Known facts. Easy shape (96499989, a466679a): verb and object, three single-mark decoys.

items.subtype: Direct question: inverted order and a question mark
items.passage: The cliffs of Staffa, a small uninhabited island in Scotland’s Inner Hebrides, consist of thousands of tall basalt columns, many of them hexagonal. Visitors often ask the same question: Why ______ The lava that formed the island contracted and fractured as it cooled, splitting into columns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: do the columns have such regular shapes?
do the columns have such regular shapes.
the columns have such regular shapes?
the columns have such regular shapes.
items.explanation: “Why do the columns have such regular shapes?” is a direct question, introduced after the colon. A direct question uses question word order, with the helping verb “do” before the subject “the columns,” and ends with a question mark.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

C.why_wrong: A direct question needs question word order (“do the columns have”); “the columns have” is statement order.

D.why_wrong: Statement word order and a period make this a statement, but the colon after “Visitors often ask the same question” and the word “Why” introduce a direct question.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Staffa, Inner Hebrides: columnar basalt from a cooling lava flow that contracted and cracked into mostly six-sided columns). Known facts. Easy shape (1f39ab8b, direct question after a colon, with the 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement order and a period
items.passage: In a 1966 study, economists William Baumol and William Bowen explained why ______ A string quartet, they observed, requires the same four musicians and the same amount of time to perform a piece as it did in the 1800s. Performers’ salaries, however, rise along with salaries elsewhere in the economy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: were the costs of live performances rising so quickly?
the costs of live performances were rising so quickly.
the costs of live performances were rising so quickly?
were the costs of live performances rising so quickly.
items.explanation: The question is embedded in a statement: the economists “explained why the costs of live performances were rising so quickly.” An embedded question uses statement word order (subject “the costs” before the verb “were rising”) and, since the whole sentence is a statement, ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: Question word order and a question mark belong to a direct question, but here the question is part of the statement “economists ... explained why ...”

C.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement about what the economists explained, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.

D.why_wrong: Question word order (“were the costs”) is wrong inside an embedded question; after “explained why,” the subject comes before the verb.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Baumol and Bowen, Performing Arts: The Economic Dilemma, 1966, the cost disease: a string quartet needs the same players and time as in the past while wages rise with the rest of the economy). Known facts. Easy shape (aab78b25: embedded question after a verb, statement order and a period).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: German artist Hannah Höch was one of the few women participating in Berlin’s Dada movement. Because her job at a publishing company gave her access to stacks of illustrated ______ Höch had a steady supply of photographs to cut apart and reassemble in her photomontages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Because her job at a publishing company gave her access to stacks of illustrated magazines” is an introductory dependent clause. A comma correctly separates it from the main clause that follows, “Höch had a steady supply of photographs ...”

A.why_wrong: With “and,” both “her job ... gave her access to stacks of illustrated magazines” and “Höch had a steady supply ...” fall under “Because,” so the sentence is left with no main clause; the comma required after the introductory clause is also missing.

B.why_wrong: A comma plus “and” coordinates two main clauses, but the “because” clause before it is dependent: the sentence either has no main clause or illogically coordinates a dependent clause with a main clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory “because” clause runs into the main clause, and “illustrated magazines Höch” reads as one phrase.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Hannah Höch, Berlin Dada, photomontage; she worked for the Ullstein publishing house from 1916 to 1926, with access to its illustrated magazines). Known facts. Easy shape (b35cefb7 menu: `content and`, `content,`, `content`, `content, and`).

items.subtype: Commas between items in a simple series
items.passage: In 1942, designers Charles and Ray Eames developed a lightweight leg splint for the US Navy. To produce it, they glued thin sheets of wood veneer ______ pressed them into a mold, and heated them until the layers hardened into a single curved piece.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three actions: “glued thin sheets of wood veneer together,” “pressed them into a mold,” and “heated them until the layers hardened ...” A comma correctly separates the first item from the second, matching the comma before “and heated.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon separates items in a series only when the items contain commas; these three simple verb phrases are separated with commas.

B.why_wrong: The period ends the sentence after the first item and leaves “And pressed them into a mold, and heated them ...” as a fragment with no subject.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, “together pressed them into a mold” runs the first two items of the series together.

items.notes: Subject: arts and design (Charles and Ray Eames, molded plywood leg splint for the US Navy, 1942, made from glued veneers pressed and heated in a mold; the technique led to their plywood chairs). Known facts. Easy shape (577b09fa menu, including its `. And` decoy: blank after the first of three verb phrases).

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that clause
items.passage: In 1964, Finnish textile designer Maija Isola created Unikko, a print of oversized red and black poppies, for the clothing manufacturer Marimekko. It was a daring choice, since Marimekko’s founder, Armi Ratia, had reportedly declared that the company would never print a ______ featured flowers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That featured flowers” is a restrictive clause: it tells which kind of pattern the company would never print, so no comma comes before “that.” “That” is needed as the subject of the verb “featured.”

B.why_wrong: A comma before “that” wrongly sets off the restrictive clause “that featured flowers,” which is essential to the meaning (the company would print patterns, just not ones with flowers).

C.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “featured” has no subject: “would never print a pattern featured flowers” is not grammatical.

D.why_wrong: Without “that,” the comma leaves “featured flowers” with no subject, and the comma separates “a pattern” from words that must describe it.

items.notes: Subject: arts and design (Maija Isola's Unikko poppy print for Marimekko, 1964, made although founder Armi Ratia had said Marimekko would never print florals). Known facts. Easy shape (cabe71d4 menu: `company,` / `company that` / `company` / `company, that`).

items.subtype: Opening comma of a pair around a nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: Cuban-born writer Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda published Sab in Madrid in 1841. The ______ which portrays an enslaved man’s devotion to his owner’s daughter, appeared eleven years before Uncle Tom’s Cabin and was banned in Cuba for its antislavery sentiments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Which portrays an enslaved man’s devotion to his owner’s daughter” is extra information about the novel, closed by the comma after “daughter.” A matching comma is needed before “which” to open the element.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “The novel” is only a subject; the verb “appeared” comes later.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “The novel” as a fragment and turns “Which portrays an enslaved man’s devotion ..., appeared ...” into a sentence with no subject for “appeared.”

C.why_wrong: Without a comma before “which,” the element closed by the comma after “daughter” has no opening mark.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda, Sab, 1841, published in Madrid, one of the first antislavery novels in Spanish, eleven years before Uncle Tom's Cabin, banned in Cuba). Known facts. Easy shape (ea8f4658 menu).
